data:
runi is a set of seventeen small Go packages for the data and AI work that shows up inside a running service: describing a column, ranking documents, getting JSON out of a language model, forecasting a series, versioning a table, deciding whether a signal has genuinely changed.
Each package is independent. Take one, take all seventeen, or copy a file out — the licence permits it and nothing depends on anything else.
User GuideInstall it, choose a package, and understand where it is meant to run. API ReferenceEvery exported symbol, generated from the source.
data.the-three-promises#The three promises:
Zero dependencies. Standard library only, in every package. go.mod has no require block, so there is no transitive tree to audit and nothing to pin.
100% coverage, enforced. Every package carries a coverage floor in CI. The floors are floors, not targets: a commit that drops a package below its floor fails, and no strong package’s coverage can pay for a weak one’s.
Measured, not asserted. Performance claims in the repository come with the benchmark that produced them and the hardware it ran on.

data.acf#ACF:
func ACF(y []float64, maxLag int) []float64 ACF returns the sample autocorrelation function of y for lags 0..maxLag. The value at index 0 is always 1. Use it to read the moving-average order: an MA(q) series has an ACF that cuts off after lag q.
A constant series has zero variance, so every autocorrelation beyond lag 0 is 0/0 and undefined. Rather than return NaNs, ACF reports lag 0 as 1 — which is true by definition and keeps the documented contract — and every later lag as 0, which reads as “no structure” to the order-selection it feeds.
Defined in arimax/acf.go.
data.difference#Difference:
func Difference(y []float64, d int) []float64 Difference applies d-th order differencing: the series of successive changes, repeated d times. It is how a trending series is made stationary, and it is the “I” in ARIMA.
Each pass shortens the series by one, so the result has len(y)−d elements. Difference(y, 0) returns a copy.
Defined in arimax/diff.go.

data.fit#Fit:
func Fit(y []float64, x []float64, k int, ord Order) (*Model, error) Fit estimates an ARIMAX model of y with optional exogenous regressors.
x is row-major with one row per observation of y and k columns, or nil for a plain ARIMA. The form fitted is regression with ARIMA errors, as described in the package documentation; the estimator is conditional least squares over the regression and ARMA parameters jointly, reached by alternating an exact generalised-least-squares solve for the coefficients on prewhitened data with a Nelder-Mead refit of the ARMA. It is not exact maximum likelihood.
Defined in arimax/arimax.go.
data.forecasting-needs-future-x#Forecasting n: This is the part that surprises people, and the package makes it explicit in the API rather than hiding it: an ARIMAX forecast h steps ahead requires the exogenous values for those h steps. Forecast takes them as an argument and returns ErrNoFutureX if they are missing. Where X is genuinely known in advance — planned spend, a published schedule, a committed price — this is a strength. Where it is not, the X forecast’s error enters the Y forecast and the prediction intervals below UNDERSTATE the true uncertainty, because they condition on X being correct. Say so wherever the output is shown.
data.how-it-is-fitted#How it is fitted:
This package uses the regression-with-ARIMA-errors formulation rather than stuffing X into a single joint likelihood:
Y_t = β’X_t + n_t where n_t follows an ARIMA(p,d,q)
The two are equivalent in what they express, but this form is far better behaved numerically and each block is separately testable. Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, recommends the same decomposition, and it is why statsmodels calls the joint variant “SARIMAX” and this one “ARIMA with exog”.

data.ljungbox#LjungBox:
func LjungBox(resid []float64, h, dof int) (q float64, df int) LjungBox computes the Ljung–Box Q statistic on the first h lags of the residual autocorrelations, with dof degrees of freedom consumed by the fitted model (p+q). A large Q means the residuals still carry structure, so the model is misspecified.
It returns Q and the degrees of freedom. The package deliberately does not return a p-value: that needs a chi-squared CDF, and shipping an approximation of one invites people to read significance off a number that is only roughly right. Compare Q against a chi-squared table with the returned dof.
Defined in arimax/acf.go.

data.measured-against-statsmodels#Measured ag:
200 independent synthetic series, ARMA(1,1) errors, one exogenous regressor, n=500, h=6, both libraries reading the same generated CSVs. The control is the naive carry-forward error, which depends on the data and on neither library: 3.7104740961972245 against 3.710474096197225, which is the same number to one unit in the last place — a difference of 1.2e-16, from the order the two languages sum 200 values in. That is how the two are known to have been fitted to identical data.
arimax SARIMAX fit, n=500 1.35 ms 15.79 ms 12x faster fit, n=2,000 4.25 ms 53.79 ms 13x faster fit, n=10,000 18.31 ms 267.83 ms 15x faster per fit over the 200 trials 1.58 ms 16.32 ms 10x faster start-up before first fit 0 ms 676 ms 95% interval coverage 94.5% 94.5% identical forecast RMSE, h=6 1.31600 1.31601 within 0.001% AR phi bias / RMSE -0.00410/0.05062 -0.00407/0.05062 beta bias / RMSE +0.00249/0.03364 +0.00229/0.03361
The exogenous coefficient used to be the row to read first: a staged fit estimated it with an RMSE of 0.06662, twice the exact-likelihood figure. With the generalised-least-squares descent described above it is 0.03364 against 0.03361 — 0.1% apart, which is well inside what 200 trials can resolve. The remaining difference between the two estimators is not visible in any figure in this table.
What the ten-fold speed margin now buys is the same answer per request rather than per batch. What it does not buy is exact ML, SARIMA, state space models, or the diagnostics statsmodels ships; where those are the job, use it.
Measured on an ASUS Ascent GX10, 20 cores, aarch64, Go 1.27.2, statsmodels 0.15.0 on Python 3.12.3. See benchmarks/README.md in the repository for the method and the raw results.

data.modelforecast#Model.Forecast:
func (m *Model) Forecast(h int, xFuture []float64, alpha float64) (point, lo, hi []float64, err error) Forecast predicts h steps beyond the fitted series.
xFuture is row-major with h rows and the same number of columns as the X used to fit, or nil when the model has no regressors. It is REQUIRED: an ARIMAX forecast cannot be produced without the exogenous values for the horizon, and this returns an error rather than silently assuming they are zero or held flat — both of which produce a confident, wrong answer.
The returned intervals are (1−alpha) prediction intervals from the model’s psi-weights. They assume Gaussian errors and KNOWN parameters, and they condition on xFuture being correct, so where xFuture is itself a forecast the true uncertainty is wider than reported.
Missing or short xFuture returns ErrNoFutureX, which wraps ErrInvalid. A Model that did not come from Fit returns ErrNotFitted. h <= 0 on a fitted model returns all nil.
Defined in arimax/arimax.go.
data.numerical-choices-stated#Numerical choic: OLS is solved by Householder QR, not by inverting X’X. Channel spend series are strongly collinear and the normal equations square the condition number. The ARMA block minimises the conditional sum of squares (CSS) by Nelder–Mead; the regression block minimises the same CSS exactly, by QR on prewhitened data. CSS conditions on the first p observations instead of running a Kalman filter for the exact likelihood. It needs no state space machinery, and for series of the length this package targets the difference from exact ML is small. It is not exact ML, and this package does not claim to be. The AR polynomial is held inside Σ|φ| < 0.999. A fit that parks on that bound is telling you the series wanted a unit root — another difference, or a drift term this package does not have — and its reported Sigma2, and so its intervals, can collapse towards zero. Check AR against the bound before believing a very narrow interval. Prediction intervals come from the MA(∞) psi-weights of the fitted model, so they widen with horizon in the right shape. They assume Gaussian errors and known parameters; they do not include parameter estimation error. Everything is deterministic: same input, same output, no concurrency, no randomness, no clock.

data.the-estimator-precisely#The estimator, p:
Both blocks are fitted against ONE objective: the conditional sum of squares of the ARIMA errors. Fit reaches it by block coordinate descent.
Ordinary least squares gives a starting β, and an ARMA fit to the regression errors gives starting φ and θ. Those φ and θ define a whitening filter. Apply it to y and to every column of [1, X] and re-solve least squares on the filtered data. Because the filter is linear with fixed zero pre-sample values, the filtered residual IS the conditional residual, so this solve is the exact minimiser of the objective over β at those φ and θ. This is feasible generalised least squares — Cochrane–Orcutt generalised from AR(1) errors to ARMA(p,q). Refit the ARMA to the new errors, warm started, and repeat from 2 until the coefficients stop moving or four passes have run. Neither half-step can raise the objective, so the whole iteration descends; TestPropertyRefineNeverRaisesTheConditionalSumOfSquares measures that rather than a runtime guard asserting it.
This matters because it is where the accuracy went. An earlier version of this package STAGED the two blocks — one least-squares solve, one ARMA fit, done — which estimates β as if the errors were independent. That is still unbiased, but it is inefficient, and on the persistent errors this package targets the inefficiency is large: with ARMA(1,1) errors at φ=0.6, θ=0.3 the variance of the staged β is about four times the generalised one, so twice the standard error. That factor was the whole of the measured accuracy gap against an exact-likelihood fit, and closing it cost a factor of three in speed out of a thirty-fold margin.
It is NOT exact maximum likelihood. The objective conditions on the first p observations and on zero pre-sample shocks instead of running a Kalman filter over the exact likelihood; the two differ by the information in those initial conditions, which is O(1) terms against a sum over n. Where d > 0 the intercept differences to zero, so it is not identified by the objective and is left at its least-squares value — harmless for forecasting, where it cancels through the integration, but it is not an estimate of a drift, and this package has no drift parameter.
data.the-model#The model:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/arimax" Package arimax fits and forecasts ARIMAX models — ARIMA with exogenous regressors — using only the Go standard library.
The modelY_t = c + Σ φ_i·Y_{t−i} + Σ θ_j·ε_{t−j} + Σ β_k·X_{t,k} + ε_t
φ are the autoregressive parameters, θ the moving-average parameters, β the coefficients on the exogenous regressors X, and ε white noise.

data.avro-is-not-ours#Avro is not ours:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/avro" Package avro is a dependency-free (standard-library-only) implementation of the Apache Avro binary encoding and the Avro Object Container File (OCF) format — enough of the spec to persist typed records to object storage in a self-describing, splittable, compressed container.
Avro is not oursApache Avro is a data serialisation format created and maintained by the Apache Software Foundation, specified at https://avro.apache.org. This package is an independent implementation of that public specification. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or a product of the Apache Software Foundation, and “Apache Avro” is their trademark, not ours. What is ours is this Go code and its bugs.
data.decoder#Decoder:
type Decoder struct Decoder reads Avro binary primitives out of a window of bytes, refilling the window from an io.Reader when it runs dry.
The window is the point. Decoding a value is a bounds check and an index into a []byte, not a ReadByte or a ReadFull through an io.Reader: an indirect call per value, plus — for every fixed-width type — a local array that escapes to the heap because it is passed as an interface argument. That overhead, not the arithmetic, is what made reading a container cost ten times what writing one did. A Decoder over bytes already in memory does no I/O at all.
Defined in avro/avro.go.

data.what-is-implemented-and-what-is-not#What:
Implemented: the binary encoding for the primitive types, records, arrays, maps, unions and enums; OCF read and write with the null and deflate codecs; the sync marker and block framing that make a file splittable.
NOT implemented: schema resolution between a writer’s and a reader’s schema, schema registries, RPC, logical types beyond what is noted in the type table, and the snappy and zstd codecs. If you need writer/reader schema evolution, this package is the wrong tool — it reads a file with the schema that file carries.
data.why-another-one#Why another one: The established Go implementations are good and carry dependencies. This one exists because the rest of this module promises zero dependencies, and a container format is not worth breaking that promise for. If you are already using github.com/hamba/avro or github.com/linkedin/goavro, they cover more of the specification than this does and you should keep using them.

data.commit#Commit: Optimistic concurrency: read the head (the _last hint, then a LIST of _log/), write the data file, then PutIfAbsent(_log/). Losing that race yields ErrExists; the writer re-reads the head and conflict-checks. Appends never conflict. A compaction conflicts when a file it removes is no longer live; it then re-plans from the new head. Retries use jittered exponential backoff, up to the limit set by WithMaxAttempts (32 by default). Versions are therefore dense: 1, 2, 3, … with no gaps.

data.encryption-is-the-stores-business-not-th:
barn does not encrypt anything. It hands bytes to the [Store] and reads them back, so whether objects are sealed at rest is entirely a property of the implementation you supply.
If you do seal them, bind the ciphertext to the object’s KEY. Every key here already encodes tenant, table and path (tables///), so binding to the key gives you the property worth having: a data file copied into another tenant’s or table’s prefix fails to open rather than being served as that table’s data. A scheme that binds only to the bucket, or to nothing, will decrypt a misplaced file happily.

data.layout#Layout:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/barn" Package barn is an append-only, versioned key/value table kept entirely on the object store — the Delta/Iceberg (“Snowflake/Databricks-style”) pattern, scaled down to application metadata. There is no database process: a table is a set of immutable Avro data files plus a transaction log of JSON entries, and the only coordination primitive is the object store’s atomic create (PutIfAbsent: an atomic create).
LayoutEverything for one table lives under tables///:
data/.avro immutable Avro OCF rows (key, op put|del, ts, payload, ver, ord) _log/%020d.json commit N: {version, parent, ts, writer, add, remove, op} _checkpoint/%020d.avro the full live file set as of version N _checkpoint/_last the newest checkpoint version — a HINT only
A data file’s name is 16 hex digits of its creation time (unix µs) followed by 32 random hex digits (crypto/rand). The time prefix lets Vacuum age an orphan without reading it and without trusting server mtimes, which many object stores do not expose.
data.memstore#MemStore:
type MemStore struct MemStore is an in-memory [Store]: the reference implementation, and enough to run a table in a test without any infrastructure.
It is NOT a toy. It implements the one guarantee the table’s correctness rests on — PutIfAbsent is an atomic create — and it is safe for concurrent use, so the optimistic-concurrency paths can be exercised honestly rather than simulated. What it is not is durable: everything is lost when it goes out of scope.
Use it to try the package, to test code that writes tables, and as the shortest correct example of what a real Store must do.

data.what-it-does-not-do#What it does not do:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/budget" Package budget splits one deadline between the phases of a piece of work, and keeps an honest record of how each phase spent its share.
A request that must answer in three minutes usually grows a timeout per step: two minutes for this call, ninety seconds for that scrape. Each number is defensible on its own, nothing adds them up, and the only real bound on the whole is whatever the client gives up at. This package replaces that with one deadline and a slice for every phase derived from what is left when the phase starts:
slice(phase) = min( cap(phase), remaining − margin − Σ floor(later stages) )
A floor is time an earlier stage may not take: give the phase that writes the answer a floor, and no amount of slowness earlier on can leave it with nothing. Phases that share a stage run concurrently, so only strictly later stages hold time back. A phase whose slice is below the plan’s MinSlice is not started at all and is recorded as skipped, rather than started into a guaranteed overrun.
b, err := budget.New(plan) ctx, cancel, ok := b.Begin(parent, “search”) if ok { err := search(ctx) cancel() b.End(ctx, “search”, err) } … for _, r := range b.Finalize() { // r did not finish: say so in the answer }
Every phase ends as done, failed, overrun or skipped. Finalize freezes that record when the answer is assembled: a phase still running then is overrun, and nothing that happens afterwards changes the record. The answer can then say which parts it is missing instead of silently leaving them out.
What it does not doIt does not schedule. It never runs, orders, retries or parallelises your phases; it answers “how long may this phase take if it starts now?” and records what happened. Stage numbers only tell it which floors are still ahead.
It does not stop work. A slice is a context deadline, and cancellation in Go is cooperative: a phase that ignores its context keeps running and keeps whatever it holds. Finalize reports it as overrun, which is true, but the goroutine is yours to stop.
Its caps are a plan, not a measurement. Nothing here knows whether a phase can finish in its slice; measure that on the hardware that will run it.
The ledger reads time through the clock you give New with WithClock, so the arithmetic can be tested with a fake clock. Context deadlines are set from durations and expire on the real clock.

data.choosing-a-hasher#Choosing a hasher:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/chain" Package chain makes a sequence of records tamper-evident: each record is sealed with a hash that covers the record before it, so changing, moving or swapping one breaks the chain at that point, and Verify says where and how.
It is for logs that must not be quietly rewritten: decisions taken on someone’s behalf, approvals, payments released. The records are yours. You give chain the bytes that stand for a record (your canonical encoding), and it keeps the links:
l1 := chain.Seal(chain.Bound, “”, body1) l2 := chain.Seal(chain.Bound, l1.Hash, body2) head, err := chain.Verify(chain.Bound, []chain.Link{l1, l2})
Verify walks the links in order and stops at the first break, reporting what kind it is:
Altered: a link’s body no longer matches its hash. It was edited after it was sealed. Reordered: a link names, as the one before it, a link that is in the chain but somewhere else. Records were moved. Replaced: a link names, as the one before it, a hash that is not in the chain at all. The record it was sealed after was swapped out or removed. Choosing a hasherBound hashes the previous link’s hash together with the body, with a domain prefix, so the link is part of what is sealed. Use it for new chains. BodyOnly hashes the body alone; use it only when your body already carries the previous hash (for example as a prev_hash field in the encoded record), which is how many existing logs are built. With BodyOnly and a body that does not carry it, the hash does not bind the order, and Verify can only catch a reorder through the Prev fields, which an editor can rewrite.

data.cusum#CUSUM:
type CUSUM struct CUSUM is the two-sided tabular cumulative-sum test for a shift in the mean away from a known target.
Each side accumulates the evidence for a shift in its direction and is floored at zero, so that time spent in control is not credited against a later shift:
S⁺t = max(0, S⁺{t−1} + x_t − target − k) S⁻t = max(0, S⁻{t−1} + target − x_t − k)
and a side signals once it exceeds h. k is the slack: deviations smaller than k drain the sum rather than feed it. Set to half the shift you want to catch, the test is the fastest possible detector for a shift of exactly that size among those with the same false-alarm rate, in the worst-case sense of Lorden (G. V. Moustakides, “Optimal stopping times for detecting changes in distributions”, Annals of Statistics 14(4), 1986). For shifts much smaller than 2k it is slow, and EWMAChart is the better choice when the size is unknown.
Since estimates when the shift began: a side becomes positive at about the sample the shift started, so the run of samples for which it has been positive is the age of the shift. This is Montgomery’s estimate, and it costs nothing to keep.

data.decayed#Decayed:
type Decayed struct Decayed turns a cumulative counter, read at irregular times, into an exponentially decayed average rate.
Many system statistics are published as running totals rather than rates: microseconds spent stalled on memory or I/O since boot, bytes sent, requests served. What a reader wants is “the share of time stalled over the last minute” or “requests per second lately”, which is what operating systems report alongside such totals as 10, 60 and 300 second averages. Decayed computes that from the totals alone. For a counter of microseconds stalled, the rate is microseconds per second, so dividing by 1e6 gives the share of time (multiply by 100 for a percentage).
Each Update takes the rate over the interval since the last one, r = Δtotal/Δt, and blends it into the average with
e = exp(−Δt/window), a = a·e + r·(1−e).
This is exact for irregular sampling: it is the continuous-time exponential average with time constant window of a rate that was r throughout the interval, which is all a pair of counter readings can say about it. A fixed per-sample weight, as in EWMA, would be wrong under jitter: a reading delayed to 3 s would count the same as one taken after 1 s, and a burst of readings close together would drag the average towards whatever those moments happened to show. Here a reading’s weight is the time it covers.
After one window of a new constant rate the average has moved 1 − 1/e, about 63%, of the way from the old rate to the new one, whatever the spacing of the readings; after three windows, 95%. The first rate initialises the average directly rather than being blended into an implicit zero, which would read as a quiet system for the first window and then as a rise that never happened.
A total lower than the previous one means the counter was reset, or wrapped past its maximum. With one reading the two cannot be told apart, so both are treated as a reset: the reading becomes a new baseline, no rate is produced, and Resets is incremented. A counter that wraps loses one interval, never yields an absurd rate.
Time comes only from the at argument; nothing here reads the clock, so it is as testable as the caller’s clock is. Intervals are taken with time.Time.Sub, which uses the monotonic reading that time.Now attaches, so a wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort the interval. Readings at or before the previous one (a clock stepped backwards, a duplicate) are skipped and counted in Skipped, and leave the baseline where it was: the next valid reading covers their interval.
Method: the exponential smoothing of irregularly spaced data of D. J. Wright, “Forecasting data published at irregular time intervals using an extension of Holt’s method”, Management Science 32(4), 1986, here applied to the interval-average rate, which makes the step response exact rather than approximate.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewDecayed. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

type EWMA struct EWMA is an exponentially weighted moving average: each new value moves the average a fixed fraction alpha of the way towards itself,
v_t = v_{t−1} + alpha·(x_t − v_{t−1}),
so a value k samples old carries weight alpha·(1−alpha)^k. It describes a level; it does not test one. For a decision about whether the level moved, use EWMAChart, which adds the control limits this lacks.
The first value initialises the average rather than being blended with an implicit zero, so a series that starts at 500 does not spend its first few dozen samples climbing up from nothing. The average counts samples, not time: for readings at irregular times, Decayed is the right tool.
Method: the exponentially weighted average as used in forecasting by R. G. Brown, Statistical Forecasting for Inventory Control, McGraw-Hill, 1959.
The zero value is not usable (its alpha is 0); build one with NewEWMA or NewEWMAHalfLife. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in Skipped.

data.ewmachart#EWMAChart:
type EWMAChart struct EWMAChart is an exponentially weighted moving average control chart: it signals when a smoothed series leaves a band around a target level.
The statistic is
z_t = λ·x_t + (1−λ)·z_{t−1}, z_0 = target,
and the band at sample t is
target ± L·σ·sqrt( λ/(2−λ) · (1 − (1−λ)^(2t)) ).
σ times the square root is the exact standard deviation of z_t when the x_t are independent with standard deviation σ. It starts at λσ and widens towards the asymptotic σ·sqrt(λ/(2−λ)); using the asymptotic band from the first sample would leave the chart nearly blind to a shift present from the start.
Use it for small shifts that persist. Averaging over about 2/λ samples lets it see a shift of half a standard deviation that a chart of raw values would never flag, at the price of reacting more slowly than a raw-value check to a single large spike. For a shift of one known size CUSUM is the faster detector; the two have similar performance across a range of sizes.
Method: S. W. Roberts, “Control chart tests based on geometric moving averages”, Technometrics 1(3), 1959. Exact-variance limits and run-length tables: J. M. Lucas and M. S. Saccucci, “Exponentially weighted moving average control schemes: properties and enhancements”, Technometrics 32(1), 1990. Presentation follows D. C. Montgomery, Introduction to Statistical Quality Control, Wiley, chapter on CUSUM and EWMA charts.
target and σ are the in-control mean and standard deviation of the series, and they are yours to supply: estimate them from a stretch you know to be normal (Welford does that), not from the stretch under test. The chart assumes independent samples; a strongly autocorrelated series inflates the spread of z_t beyond what the limits allow for and signals too often.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewEWMAChart or DefaultEWMAChart. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in Skipped, and do not advance t. Finite inputs within a factor of a few of the float64 limit can overflow z_t; rescale such a series first.

data.pagehinkley#PageHinkley:
type PageHinkley struct PageHinkley is the Page–Hinkley test for a change in the mean of a series whose level is not known in advance.
It is CUSUM with the target replaced by the running mean of everything seen since the last Reset. With mean_t the mean of x_1..x_t, it keeps
m⁺_t = Σ (x_i − mean_i − δ), M⁺_t = min(0, m⁺_1, …, m⁺_t) m⁻_t = Σ (x_i − mean_i + δ), M⁻_t = max(0, m⁻_1, …, m⁻_t)
and signals Up when m⁺_t − M⁺_t > λ and Down when M⁻_t − m⁻_t > λ (the larger when both, Up on a tie). δ plays the part of CUSUM’s k, the size of deviation tolerated without accumulating evidence, and λ the part of h.
Use it when there is no target to supply: a series per process, per disk, per tenant, each settling at its own level. The price is that the reference level is learned from the series itself. Shortly after Reset it rests on a handful of samples, so the test is noisier than CUSUM with a true target. After a change the running mean slowly absorbs the new level, the evidence stops growing and then drains, and the next change would be measured against a blend of both regimes. Reset after acting on a signal. When the target is known, CUSUM is the sharper test.
Method: E. S. Page, “Continuous inspection schemes”, Biometrika 41(1/2), 1954; D. V. Hinkley, “Inference about the change-point from cumulative sum tests”, Biometrika 58(3), 1971. The running-mean formulation is the one given by J. Gama, I. Žliobaitė, A. Bifet, M. Pechenizkiy and A. Bouchachia, “A survey on concept drift adaptation”, ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), 2014.
δ and λ are in the data’s units and the caller’s to choose. There is no literature default worth the name, since both scale with the noise. δ = σ/2 and λ = 5σ, the CUSUM defaults, are a reasonable start: at those values the in-control average run length measured here is about 480 samples, close to CUSUM’s 465, and a one-sigma shift after 100 in-control samples is detected in about 11 to 12 (TestPageHinkleyARL). The delay grows when the shift comes early, while the mean still rests on few samples.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewPageHinkley. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in Skipped. Finite inputs within a factor of a few of the float64 limit can overflow the sums; rescale such a series first.

data.welford#Welford:
type Welford struct Welford is a running mean and variance in one pass and fixed memory.
The obvious one-pass method keeps Σx and Σx² and takes (Σx² − (Σx)²/n)/(n−1) at the end. On data far from zero that subtracts two nearly equal huge numbers, and the variance it returns is mostly rounding: readings that move by a few units around 1e9 lose every significant digit of their spread, and the result can even come out negative. Welford’s update keeps the mean and the sum of squared deviations from it instead, so nothing large is ever subtracted from anything large.
Method: B. P. Welford, “Note on a method for calculating corrected sums of squares and products”, Technometrics 4(3), 1962. Merge is the pairwise combination of T. F. Chan, G. H. Golub and R. J. LeVeque, “Updating formulae and a pairwise algorithm for computing sample variances”, Stanford report STAN-CS-79-773, 1979, published as “Algorithms for computing the sample variance: analysis and recommendations”, The American Statistician 37(3), 1983.
The zero value is an empty accumulator, ready to use. A Welford is a plain value and safe to copy, which is how a snapshot is taken; it is not safe for concurrent use. NaN and ±Inf are skipped and counted in Skipped, never folded in: one NaN would otherwise poison the mean for the rest of the series. Finite values whose squared spread overflows float64 (beyond about 1e154) give a variance of +Inf, never NaN or a negative number; the mean stays finite. data.what-this-package-does-not-do#What this:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/drift" Package drift tells you when a stream of measurements has changed regime.
It is for series read from a running system over and over — a pressure stall percentage every second, a latency per request, a queue depth per scrape — where the question is “has this moved?” and the answer is needed as each reading arrives. Every type does O(1) work and holds fixed memory per update, allocates nothing, and is a plain value, so one detector per series is affordable for thousands of series.
Which to use:
Welford and EWMA describe. Welford is the exact running mean and variance, numerically stable and mergeable across shards; EWMA is a smoothed level that forgets. Neither decides anything. Welford over a known-good stretch is how to get the target and σ the detectors need. EWMAChart catches small shifts that persist — half a standard deviation, sustained — that a check on raw values never sees, and is a good general choice when the size of the shift you care about is unknown. CUSUM catches a shift of a size you name, and for that size it is the fastest detector there is at a given false-alarm rate. It also estimates when the shift began (Since). PageHinkley is CUSUM for when you have no target: the reference level is the series’ own running mean. Decayed is not a detector. It turns a cumulative counter (time stalled, bytes sent) read at irregular times into a decayed rate — the “average over the last 10/60/300 s” that operating systems publish — which is usually the series you then want to watch. The detectors return a Signal: Up, Down or None, for the sample just added. A signal is a statistic crossing a threshold you chose; what follows from it is your code’s decision, and the detector carries on accumulating until you call Reset.
c, _ := drift.DefaultCUSUM(target, sigma) for x := range readings { if s := c.Add(x); s != drift.None { log.Printf("%s shift began %d samples ago", s, c.Since()) c.Reset() } }
Every type skips NaN and ±Inf rather than folding them in, and counts them: a missed reading should not poison a statistic for the rest of the series, and a series that is mostly NaN should be visible as one (Skipped). None is safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or guard it.
What this package does not doIt does not choose thresholds. The defaults offered (DefaultCUSUM, DefaultEWMAChart) are the textbook values, with the false-alarm rates the textbooks give for them, stated in their docs and checked by tests. Whether a false alarm every 465 samples suits a series read every second is a question about your system, not about statistics.
It does not know about seasons. A daily cycle is, to every detector here, a shift up every morning and down every night. Remove the cycle first — the residual from github.com/org-runink/runi/season is the series to watch — or compare against the same hour of previous days yourself.
It is univariate. Each detector watches one series. Shifts that show only in the relationship between series (two latencies that normally move together diverging) need a multivariate chart such as Hotelling’s T² or MEWMA, which this package does not provide.
Signals are not probabilities. A CUSUM over h says the evidence crossed h; it does not say “99% sure”. The in-control average run lengths in the docs are the honest way to read the rate of false alarms, and they assume independent samples: on autocorrelated data every detector here signals more often than its documented rate. Model the autocorrelation away first (github.com/org-runink/runi/arimax residuals) if it is strong.
It never acts. Nothing here alerts, throttles, restarts or retries; it returns numbers.

data.why-not-synconcevalue#Why not sync.OnceV:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/lazy" Package lazy provides deferred values that can be started early.
A lazy value computes at most once, on demand. That trades latency for not doing unnecessary work: nothing is computed until something forces it, and then the forcing caller waits the full cost.
This package adds the missing half. Start begins the computation in the background without forcing it, so by the time a caller needs the value the work may already be done:
v := lazy.New(func(ctx context.Context) (Report, error) { return build(ctx) // 200ms }) v.Start(ctx) // returns immediately; work proceeds … do other things … r, err := v.Get(ctx) // ~0 if Start had time to finish
Laziness decides WHETHER work happens. Starting decides WHEN. Keeping them separate means a pipeline can stay lazy — a value that is never needed is never computed, even if Start was called and the result discarded — while the values you know you will need are already in flight.
Why not sync.OnceValueThe standard library’s sync.OnceValue and sync.OnceValues cover compute-once well, and if that is all you need, use them. This package exists for three things they do not do:
context: Get takes a ctx, so a caller can stop waiting without stopping the computation that other callers are also waiting on; speculative start: the latency optimisation above; composition: Map and Then build a graph of deferred values, so an expensive dependency is computed once and shared by everything downstream rather than once per consumer.

import "github.com/org-runink/runi/memo" Package memo is an in-process memoization cache with single-flight coalescing, TTL expiry and LRU eviction, using only the standard library.
It is built for the case where the same expensive call — an LLM completion, a tool invocation, a rate-limited API request — is made repeatedly with identical inputs, and the work can be skipped.
c := memo.New[string, Answer](memo.Options{Capacity: 4096, TTL: 10 * time.Minute}) ans, err := c.Do(ctx, key, func(ctx context.Context) (Answer, error) { return expensive(ctx, req) })
Why single-flight is part of the cache, not beside itA plain cache helps the SECOND caller. Under concurrency the problem is usually the first N callers arriving together on a cold key: each misses, each runs the expensive call, and the cache turns an N-fold stampede into an N-fold stampede that also writes N times. Do coalesces them — one execution, every caller gets its result. The two mechanisms cover different populations (sequential repeats, concurrent duplicates) and neither substitutes for the other, so this package does both rather than leaving the second to the caller.
Errors are not cached by defaultCaching a failure converts a transient fault into a sticky one for the whole TTL, and this is the single most common way a memo cache makes a system worse rather than better. By default a call returning a non-nil error is not stored, though it IS still coalesced, so a thundering herd against a failing dependency still produces one call rather than N. Set CacheErrors to override that deliberately.
What this is not Not distributed. It is per-process, with no network and no shared state. Two replicas have two caches. That is a property, not an oversight: the moment a cache is shared it needs invalidation, coherence and a failure mode of its own. Not a semantic cache. Keys match exactly. There is no embedding, no similarity threshold, and therefore no possibility of returning a confidently wrong answer because two different requests looked alike. Not a persistence layer. Nothing survives a restart. Determinism and testingExpiry reads a clock that can be injected (Options.Now), so tests advance time rather than sleeping. Everything else is deterministic.
Measured against functools.lru_cacheSame experiment on both sides: N callers hit one cold key simultaneously, the function takes 5 ms, and what is counted is how many times the function actually ran.
memo lru_cache cache hit 19.6 ns 36.6 ns cache miss 725 ns 82 ns lru_cache 8.8x faster 8 cold callers, function ran 1 8 64 cold callers, function ran 1 64 wall clock, 64 cold callers 5.75 ms 13.17 ms TTL yes no single-flight yes no
The miss is genuinely slower: lru_cache inserts into a dict keyed on the argument tuple’s hash, while this one canonicalises a structured key and maintains an LRU list and expiry. The row that matters is the count. With 64 callers on a cold key lru_cache calls the expensive function 64 times and this calls it once, so if that function is a model inference or a metered API call the difference is not 8.8x on a nanosecond but 64x on the expensive thing. That is not a flaw in lru_cache, which never promised single-flight.
Measured on an ASUS Ascent GX10, 20 cores, aarch64, Go 1.27.2, Python 3.12.3.

Hash func Hash(parts ...any) string Hash builds a deterministic cache key from structured parts.
The hard part of an exact-match cache is not storage, it is deciding that two requests are the same request. Hash makes that decision explicit and repeatable:
map keys are SORTED before hashing, because Go randomises map iteration order and hashing a map directly would produce a different key every run for identical input — a cache that never hits and never tells you why; values are TYPE-TAGGED, so Hash(“1”) and Hash(1) and Hash(true) differ. Untagged concatenation collides in ways that are very hard to find later; lengths are written before variable-length data, so {“ab”,“c”} and {“a”,“bc”} do not collide. It returns a hex SHA-256. Use it for the key type of a Store:
key := memo.Hash(“model-v3”, 0.2, map[string]any{“q”: q, “lang”: “en”})
Supported typesHash encodes these types directly: nil, string, []byte, bool, every int and uint type, float32, float64, []string, []any, map[string]any and map[string]string, nested to any depth through the last four. Signed integers of every width hash alike, as do unsigned integers of every width and float32 with the float64 it converts to. Every NaN hashes alike, and -0 hashes as 0.
For these types the output is stable: the same parts give the same key in every process, on every platform, and in every v1 release of this module, so a key may be persisted or shared between processes.
Other typesAny other type is walked by reflection and hashed by its contents, never by its address: a pointer by what it points to (a nil pointer differs from a pointer to the zero value), a struct by all of its fields, exported or not, slices, arrays and maps (keys of any type, sorted) element by element, and an interface by the value it holds, tagged as if that value had been passed to Hash directly. A type that implements encoding.TextMarshaler is hashed by its text instead, so a time.Time is hashed as the instant it names and not its location pointer or monotonic reading. The type’s name and package path are part of the key, so equal contents of two types differ, and a cyclic value is hashed as a cycle rather than recursing forever. Channels, funcs and unsafe pointers have no contents and are hashed by identity: such a key matches only the same channel or func, and funcs are identified by their code, so two closures of one function literal share a key. Leave them out of keys.
Keys of these types are deterministic across runs of one build, but they are not covered by the stability promise above: renaming or moving a type, or changing its fields, changes its keys, and so may a later release of this module. Do not persist them beyond the life of a deployment.
A value of a supported type cycling through itself, such as a []any that contains itself, is not detected and overflows the stack.

data.counter#Counter:
type Counter struct Counter turns successive readings of a cumulative counter into per-interval increases and rates, across wraps and resets.
A counter of width w bits counts modulo 2^w: after 2^w − 1 it wraps to 0 and carries on, as RFC 2578 §7.1.6 defines for SNMP’s Counter32 (“when it reaches a maximum value of 2^32-1 … it wraps around and starts increasing again from zero”). Many kernel and device counters behave the same way at 32 bits, and most modern ones at 64. When a reading is below the previous one, the increase across one wrap is (2^w − previous) + total, which is (total − previous) mod 2^w.
But a reading below the previous one is also what a reset looks like: the device, process or kernel restarted and the counter began again from zero. Two readings cannot tell a wrap from a reset to a small number, so Counter uses a heuristic, and it is only that: a decrease is taken as a wrap when the increase it implies is at most half the modulus, 2^(w−1), and as a reset otherwise. Put the other way round, a fall of less than half the range is a reset and a fall of half the range or more is a wrap. The reasoning is the standard assumption that the counter is read often enough to wrap at most once per interval: a reader that keeps to it comfortably sees increases well below half the range, so a wrap implying more than that is more likely a reset. The rule is wrong both ways at the margin. A genuine wrap by more than half the range is taken as a reset, and that interval is lost. A reset of a counter that stood in the top half of its range is taken as a wrap when the new total is at least half the range below the old one, and that interval’s increase is overstated by up to half the range. Read the counter often enough that it moves by well under half its range between readings: a 32-bit octet counter on a 10 Gbit/s link (1.25e9 bytes per second) wraps every 3.4 s and must be read at least every 1.7 s, which is why RFC 2863 defines 64-bit “high capacity” interface counters. Where a counter is known not to wrap in practice, width 64 makes every decrease a reset.
A 64-bit counter is never taken to have wrapped: every decrease is a reset. At 100 Gbit/s, 1.25e10 bytes per second, a 64-bit byte counter wraps once in 2^64 / 1.25e10 ≈ 1.5e9 s, about 47 years; a 64-bit count of nanoseconds of CPU time wraps once in 584 years of one CPU’s time. No interval between two readings is that long, and a decrease is a restart.
The first reading, and the first after a reset, is a baseline and yields no rate. A reading whose time is not after the previous one (a duplicate, a clock stepped backwards) is skipped and counted in Skipped, leaving the baseline where it was: the next valid reading covers its interval. A total above 2^w − 1 cannot come from a w-bit counter; it is skipped and counted in Invalid, before any other check, and also leaves the baseline alone. Intervals come from time.Time.Sub, which uses the monotonic reading that time.Now attaches, so a wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort them.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewCounter. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

data.intervals#Intervals:
type Intervals struct Intervals summarises the gaps between reading times: the last, the mean, the shortest and the longest.
A rate is only as good as the readings behind it. A poller that should read every second but is itself starved for CPU reads every five, and the rates it reports are then five-second averages that hide every burst shorter than that; a producer that has stalled sends nothing, and the next reading covers the whole stall. Watching the gaps shows both: Late says the last gap exceeded what you expect, Max shows the worst since Reset, and a Mean well below the nominal period shows readings arriving in bursts.
The mean is exact: the sum of the gaps is held as a 128-bit integer count of nanoseconds and divided by N only when Mean is called, truncating to the nanosecond. Each gap is at most math.MaxInt64 ns, so 2^63 gaps of the largest size still sum to under 2^126: the sum cannot overflow for any input, and nothing is lost to rounding as a running float64 mean would.
The first time is a baseline. A time not after the previous one (a duplicate, a clock stepped backwards, readings delivered out of order) is skipped, counted in Skipped, and leaves the baseline where it was, so the next valid time’s gap covers it. Gaps come from time.Time.Sub, which uses the monotonic reading that time.Now attaches, and like it saturate at about 292 years.
Late can only judge a gap that has closed. A producer that stops entirely never calls Add, and Late keeps reporting the gap before it; to see a gap that is still open, compare the current time with the time of your last reading.
The zero value is empty and ready to use. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

data.what-this-package-does-not-do#What this:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/rate" Package rate turns cumulative counters into per-interval rates, and keeps bounded-memory summaries of those rates.
Many system statistics are published as running totals rather than rates: bytes and packets sent, CPU time in nanoseconds, time stalled in microseconds, context switches. A poller reads each total on every tick and wants the rate over the tick, together with a short memory of what the rate has been: the highest and lowest of the last minute, the peak since the last report, whether the poller itself is keeping time. Nothing here sleeps or reads the clock: the caller passes each reading with the time it was taken, so every type is as testable as the caller’s clock is. Every update does O(1) work (amortised, for Window) in fixed memory and allocates nothing.
Which to use:
Counter turns successive totals into a Reading: the increase, the interval it covers, and the increase per second. It knows the counter’s width, so a 32-bit counter that wraps past its maximum still yields the right increase, and it tells a wrap from a reset (the counter restarted from zero) by how large the increase would have to be. Window is the minimum and maximum of the last n values, exact, in amortised O(1) per value: “the highest rate in the last 60 readings”. Peak is the maximum since you last called Reset, and when it happened: “the peak since the last report”. Intervals watches the gaps between readings rather than the readings: a producer that has stalled shows up as a long last interval, one that is bursting as a short mean. Rates here are raw: the rate over one interval, no smoothing. For a rate that forgets gradually — the 10, 60 and 300 second averages operating systems publish beside such totals — use Decayed from github.com/org-runink/runi/drift, which takes the same totals directly. Use Counter when you need each interval’s own rate (to keep a peak or a windowed maximum, to export it, to feed a detector), or when the counter is narrower than 64 bits and wraps: Decayed treats every decrease as a reset.
c, _ := rate.NewCounter(32) w, _ := rate.NewWindow(60) for tick := range ticks { if r, ok := c.Update(readOctets(), tick); ok { w.Add(r.PerSecond) } } log.Printf(“busiest second of the last minute: %.0f B/s”, w.Max())
Every type that takes float64 values skips NaN and ±Inf rather than folding them in, and counts them in Skipped: a missed reading should not poison a summary, and a series that is mostly NaN should be visible as one. Readings whose time is not after the previous reading are skipped and counted too. Counter, Peak and Intervals are plain values, safe to copy; NewWindow returns a *Window, which holds its buffer by reference and is shared, not copied. None is safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or guard it.
What this package does not doIt cannot see more than two readings say. A counter read once per interval that wraps twice in that interval, or wraps once by more than half its range, or is reset and then climbs past its old value before the next reading, gives a wrong increase or none, and nothing in the readings can show it. Read a counter often enough that it cannot move by half its range between two readings; Counter’s doc gives the arithmetic.
It does not smooth, forecast or alert. A Reading is the rate over one interval, as noisy as the interval is short; for smoothing see drift.Decayed and drift.EWMA, and for “has this rate changed?” the detectors in drift.
Window counts readings, not time. “The last 60 values” is “the last minute” only when readings arrive once a second; under irregular polling a time window would need to hold a variable number of values, which this package does not do in fixed memory.
It does not interpolate. A rate is attributed to the whole interval it was measured over; a burst inside the interval is averaged over it, and a peak shorter than the polling interval is never seen at its full height.
It does not read counters. Where the totals come from — files, sockets, device registers — is the caller’s business.
data.window#Window:
type Window struct Window is the minimum and maximum of the last Size values added, exact, in amortised O(1) time per value and fixed memory.
Rescanning the last n values on every Add costs O(n) per value; a sorted structure costs O(log n). Window keeps instead two monotonic queues of candidates. A value can only ever be the window’s maximum if no later value is at least as large, so when x arrives every queued maximum candidate ≤ x is dropped from the back, and a candidate that has left the window is dropped from the front. What remains is decreasing from front to back, its front is the maximum, and each value enters and leaves each queue once: amortised O(1), and at most Size candidates per queue. The minimum is the mirror image.
Method: the monotonic wedge of D. Lemire, “Streaming maximum-minimum filter using no more than three comparisons per element”, Nordic Journal of Computing 13(4), 2006. The block method of J. Gil and M. Werman, “Computing 2-D min, median, and max filters”, IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 15(5), 1993, reaches a similar constant cost per value, but it processes values in blocks of the window size and so answers late for a stream; the wedge answers after every value.
Ties: when x equals a queued candidate, the older one is dropped and x is kept, because x stays in the window longer and the queue stays shorter. Equal values are interchangeable, so which is kept never changes Min or Max; +0 and −0 compare equal and either may be returned for the other.
The window counts accepted values: NaN and ±Inf are skipped, counted in Skipped, and do not take a slot, so “the last 60 values” means the last 60 finite ones.
Both queues live in one buffer of 2·Size slots, 16 bytes each, allocated by NewWindow; Add and Reset never allocate. NewWindow returns a pointer, and a Window is used through it: a copy of the struct would share the buffer with the original, and using both would corrupt both. Build one per series with NewWindow.
The zero value is not usable (Add panics on it); build one with NewWindow. Not safe to copy and not safe for concurrent use.

data.what-it-does-not-do#What it does not do:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/salvage" Package salvage gets JSON out of text that was supposed to be JSON and is not quite: a language model’s reply.
Ask a model for a JSON object and you will mostly get one, wrapped in something: a markdown code fence, a sentence of preamble (“Sure! Here is the analysis:”), a closing remark, two objects where you asked for one, or an array where you asked for an object. encoding/json rightly refuses all of it. The usual fix is a regular expression from the first “{” to the last “}”, which breaks as soon as the prose contains a brace, a string contains one, or the reply holds two values.
This package scans instead of matching. It walks the text once, honouring JSON string literals and escapes, and yields every top-level balanced object or array in order:
var a Analysis if err := salvage.Decode(reply, &a); err != nil { // nothing in the reply decoded as an Analysis }
Decode tries the whole text first, then each candidate in order, and stops at the first one that decodes into the destination with no trailing data. Candidates returns the raw values if you want to choose yourself.
What it does not doIt extracts; it never repairs. A trailing comma, single-quoted strings, unquoted keys, comments, NaN, or a reply cut off mid-object are not fixed, and such a value is skipped. A “repaired” document is a guess about what the model meant, and a plausible guess that decodes is worse than an honest failure. If you need repair, ask the model again.
A candidate that decodes is only well-formed, not correct: Decode does not check that required fields are present or values are sensible. Validate what you decoded. By default unknown fields are ignored, as encoding/json does; use DecodeStrict to treat a value with unknown fields as not a match.

import "github.com/org-runink/runi/season" Package season finds the repeating pattern in a series and the points where its trend breaks, and splits the series into trend, season and residual.
It is the classical additive decomposition
y(t) = trend(t) + season(t) + residual(t)
with a piecewise-linear trend and a Fourier-series season. Each piece is usable on its own: Period answers “does this repeat, and how often?”, FitFourier models one known season, Changepoints finds trend breaks, and Decompose runs all three together and can extend the result forward.
Classical is the second, cheaper entry point, for when the period is already known: the textbook moving-average decomposition, the operation statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.seasonal_decompose performs, computed in one pass. No period detection, no trend breaks, no forecast, and about forty times less work than Decompose.
This is not Prophet. Prophet is Meta’s forecasting library; it fits a related model with a Bayesian treatment of changepoints, holidays and several seasonalities at once. If you want Prophet, use Prophet. This package is the textbook decomposition underneath, with no dependencies.
Isolated outliers are filtered out of what the estimators measure, but not out of what they return. Every estimate here is a sum of squares, so one bad reading of magnitude a contributes a² and outvotes the rest of the series: unguarded, a single spike is enough to hide a weekly season completely and to be reported as two structural breaks around itself. So Period, Changepoints and Decompose score on a copy with isolated spikes replaced by their local median, while the trend, season and residual they report are fitted to the series as given. A bad day therefore still shows up as a large Residual, where a caller looking for anomalies can find it, instead of being smoothed away. A shift in level that LASTS is a break, not an outlier, and survives the filter. Classical is the one exception, and says so in its own doc: there the moving average IS the estimate, and filtering it would make the result disagree with every other implementation of the classical decomposition.
Limits, stated so they are not discovered later:
One seasonality. A series with both a weekly and a yearly cycle gets the strongest one only. The trend is least-squares lines between changepoints, fitted independently: it may jump at a changepoint (a level shift is a break), and a forecast extends the last line. Short series are refused rather than guessed at: Period needs MinPeriodLength (28) points and two full cycles, Decompose needs 4 points, Classical needs two full cycles of the period it is given. 28 is not arbitrary — it is the shortest series in which a cycle can in fact be found, because the bar a lag must clear rises as the series shortens while the autocorrelation estimator’s ceiling falls, and below 28 the bar sits above the ceiling. A spike only a few times the noise is indistinguishable from the noise, and is neither filtered nor reliably detected. The filter earns its keep on spikes well clear of the noise, which is where the damage was. No uncertainty intervals. Measured against statsmodelsClassical computes what statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.seasonal_decompose computes, by the same method, and it is FASTER: n=4,000 at period 24 takes 0.0213 ms here against 0.1815 ms there, 8.5x faster, with the two agreeing to 2e-13 on a series of magnitude 300 — a few ulps of float64, which is to say they produce the same numbers. That is the like-for-like row, and it is the one to quote.
Decompose used to be 5x SLOWER than seasonal_decompose. It is now slightly faster — 0.155 ms against 0.1815 ms with the same period and the trend-break search off — but it is still doing a different and larger job, solving two least-squares systems where a moving average takes two additions a point. It is the wrong tool for a decomposition whose period you already know — that is what Classical is for — and the right one for the three things a moving average cannot do at all. Each piece costs what it costs:
Classical, period given 0.0213 ms Decompose, period given, no breaks 0.155 ms plus the BIC changepoint search 16.9 ms (the default) plus detecting the period too 53.5 ms Period detection on its own 3.54 ms
So: a moving average cannot tell you the period, cannot tell you where the trend broke, and cannot extrapolate. Those three are what the extra time buys, and when you need none of them, Classical is the function.
Measured on an ASUS Ascent GX10, 20 cores, aarch64, Go 1.27.2, statsmodels 0.15.0 on Python 3.12.3.

Changepoints func Changepoints(x []float64, maxK int) []int Changepoints returns up to maxK indices where the trend of x breaks, in ascending order.
It splits greedily, each time where one straight line becomes two with the largest drop in squared error. A split is kept only if that drop exceeds 3·σ²·ln(n), a BIC-style price for the two extra parameters and the break’s position, with the noise level σ estimated robustly from the median absolute deviation of first differences. Without that price every split of a noisy line looks like an improvement, and breaks are invented in smooth data. Segments are at least minSegment points long. NaN values are forward-filled.

Classical func Classical(x []float64, period int) (*Decomposition, error) Classical splits x into trend, season and residual by the classical moving-average method, in one pass over the series.
It is the textbook decomposition, and it is exactly what statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.seasonal_decompose(x, period=period, model=“additive”) computes: a centred moving average over one period is the trend, the detrended series averaged by phase is the season, and the season is then centred on zero so that it carries no level. For an EVEN period the average is taken over period+1 points with half weight at each end, because a window of 24 hourly points has no centre and a plain average of it would be assigned half an hour off; for an odd period it is the plain average of period points. The two implementations agree to 2e-13 on the interior of series of magnitude 300 — a few ulps of float64, the only disagreement left being the order the additions happen in — checked against statsmodels 0.15.0 over six series by benchmarks/verify_classical.py.
It is O(n) — a running window sum, then one pass to average by phase — where Decompose solves two least-squares systems: n=4,000 at period 24 takes 0.0213 ms against Decompose’s 0.155 ms for the same arguments, and 0.1815 ms for seasonal_decompose. It is the fast path when the period is already known.
What it does NOT do, and what Decompose is for:
No period detection. The period you pass is the period used; a wrong one is fitted without complaint. Period answers “does this repeat, and how often?”, and Decompose runs it for you. No trend breaks. The returned Changepoints is always nil. A level shift is smeared across one window of the moving average rather than reported. No forecast. The result carries no trend model, so Forecast returns nil: a moving average says nothing about the point after the last one. No outlier filtering. The average IS the estimate here, so a spike lands in the trend for the period around it and in the season for its phase. Decompose scores on a Hampel-cleaned copy; this does not, because the classical decomposition is defined without it and filtering would make the result disagree with every other implementation of it. The endsA centred average of period points is undefined for the first and last period/2 points, because there is no window to average: that is a property of the method, not of this implementation. statsmodels returns NaN there. This returns the nearest defined average instead — the leading period/2 points all hold the first real average, the trailing period/2 all hold the last — because a NaN in a component poisons the sum, the plot and the variance a caller computes from it, while a held value is a stated approximation.
Two consequences, both deliberate. The season is averaged over the interior ONLY, so those held points do not pull it towards the series’ own curvature, which is what keeps the figures identical to statsmodels. And the residual is x − trend − season at every index, so the three components add up to the series everywhere including the ends: the held trend’s error lands in the residual, visible, rather than being hidden in a smoothed trend. Those first and last period/2 residuals are therefore not comparable with the interior ones — they carry up to half a period of trend curvature. Treat the interior [period/2, len(x)−period/2) as the decomposition and the ends as padding.
NaN values are forward-filled and leading NaNs take the first real value, as everywhere else in this package. A period below 2 is an error, and so is a series shorter than two full cycles (ErrTooShort): with less than that, some phase of the season has no point at all to average.

func Decompose(x []float64, opt Options) (*Decomposition, error) Decompose splits x into trend + season + residual.
The order matters and is fixed: the period is found on the differenced series; a season is fitted after removing a straight line whose slope is the median rise over one full period (a seasonal Theil–Sen line), so neither the season nor a spike can tilt it; changepoints are found after removing that season (so the season is not mistaken for breaks); then the trend is refitted between them and the season refitted once on what the trend leaves. Both season fits clean outliers by comparing each point with the same phase in neighbouring cycles rather than with its neighbours in time, so a spike is removed and a sharp feature that recurs every cycle is kept. NaN values are forward-filled, and leading NaNs take the first real value.

It looks for the highest PEAK in the autocorrelation of the once-differenced series (differencing removes a linear trend, which would otherwise correlate with itself at every lag). A lag counts only if its autocorrelation clears a bar that rises as the series shortens and is raised for the number of lags tried, so white noise yields a season under 1% of the time, and only if at least two full cycles fit in the series. The bar is never below 0.2. The winner is then checked against its neighbours by seasonal fit, which settles off-by-one peaks. maxPeriod caps the search; 0 means half the series. data.is-it-real#Is it real?:
A correlation or a slope is an effect size: how strong a relationship looks, not how likely it is to be there at all. Two independent random series of four points clear |r| >= 0.5 about half the time by luck; at twenty points it is about 2.5%. So the effect sizes here come with their evidence:
c, ok := stats.Correlate(a, b) // r, n and the two-sided p-value t := stats.Trend(y) // OLS slope, standard error, t and p q, keep := stats.BenjaminiHochberg(ps, 0.05) // across a whole family of tests
[Correlate] refuses (ok=false) below [MinCorrelationSamples] aligned points, where a bare r misleads more than it informs. Testing many pairs at once compounds a per-test 5% error rate, so [Adjust] applies Benjamini–Hochberg, which controls the expected share of false findings among those kept. Every “not enough evidence” case returns p = 1, never 0 or NaN, so a caller that forgets to check still does the conservative thing.
These are tests against zero (no correlation, no slope) under the usual Pearson and OLS assumptions, including independent observations. Two series that both trend will correlate whether or not they are related: detrend before you Correlate them. Nothing here tests causation. The Student-t tail comes from the regularised incomplete beta function (the standard library has no t-distribution), pinned by the tests to published critical values and to reference values within a relative error of 1e-9.

type MinMaxScaler struct MinMaxScaler rescales a column onto [0,1] by its observed range.
It is the right choice when a bounded input is required and the wrong choice when outliers matter: one extreme value compresses everything else toward a single point. [Standardiser] is more robust to that; neither is robust to a value outside the fitted range, which Transform will map outside [0,1] rather than clip. Clipping silently would hide that the new data does not look like the training data, which is usually the most useful thing to know.

A struct literal or one filled in by json.Unmarshal is unfitted and its methods return [ErrNotFitted]. data.the-one-opinion#The one opinion:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/stats" Package stats is the first ten minutes of a data problem: look at the numbers, split them, scale them, and check whether two columns move together.
It exists because Go’s standard library has none of this, and a data scientist arriving from pandas or scikit-learn hits that wall immediately. Nothing here is novel; all of it is textbook. The value is that it is correct, documented about its edges, and has no dependencies.
The one opinionScalers are FITTED and then APPLIED. [Standardiser] and [MinMaxScaler] are computed from training data and then applied, unchanged, to validation and test data:
sc := stats.FitStandardiser(train) trainZ, err := sc.Transform(train) if err != nil { return err // ErrNotFitted: train was empty } testZ, err := sc.Transform(test) // the TRAINING mean and sd, deliberately
Re-fitting on the test set leaks its distribution into the model and makes every score that follows too optimistic. That mistake is easy to make and impossible to see in the output, so the API makes the correct thing the obvious thing: there is no function that scales a slice in one step.

func Trend(y []float64) TrendTest Trend fits y against its index (0, 1, 2, …) by ordinary least squares and tests the slope against zero. P is 1 when the series is too short for a residual variance (n < 3) or is constant; an exact non-flat line has P = 0.
A slope is never “rising” just because it is not exactly zero: on noise the fitted slope is essentially never zero. Use Rising and Falling, which ask the test.
A NaN anywhere in y propagates: Slope, StdErr and T come back NaN and P comes back 1, so Rising and Falling are both false. Trend does not drop or interpolate missing values, because which of those is right depends on what the gap means, and it is not a decision this function can make for the caller. Clean the series first, or check the result with math.IsNaN. The one thing Trend will not do is report a defined standard error for a series it could not measure.

data.band#Band:
type Band struct Band classifies each reading into one of an ordered set of levels — below, inside and above a band; normal, warning and critical — with hysteresis at every boundary.
The levels are numbered 0 to len(edges), lowest values first, and edge k separates level k from level k+1. Each edge is a Schmitt trigger with its own pair of levels, so a reading that sits near a boundary does not flip between the levels on either side of it: noise whose peak-to-peak amplitude is less than an edge’s Up − Down cannot carry the level across that edge both ways. A reading may move the level several steps at once; a reading strictly between an edge’s Down and Up leaves that edge where it was.
For a band where the middle is normal, give two edges: level 0 is below, 1 inside, 2 above. For severities that rise with the value, level 0 is normal and each edge is a more severe alarm; for severities that rise as the value falls, number them from the top (severity = len(edges) − level).
The edges must be in order: both Up and Down strictly increasing from one edge to the next. Then the level is always the number of edges whose trigger is on, as if each edge were a separate Hysteresis, and the tests hold Band to exactly that.
Dwell is an optional minimum time at a level after a change, as for Hysteresis: a reading less than dwell after the last change cannot move the level, is counted in Held, and is not remembered. It applies only after a change; the first move from level 0 is never delayed. With a dwell, the level is no longer the count of separate triggers, since one change holds back every edge.
The level starts at 0. NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped, and so are readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading; both are counted in Skipped and leave no other trace.
Method: the multi-level alarm with a deadband on each setpoint of ANSI/ISA-18.2-2016, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries; each edge is the trigger of O. H. Schmitt, “A thermionic trigger”, Journal of Scientific Instruments 15(1), 1938.
NewBand copies the edges; Update never changes them, so a copy of a Band shares them safely and is independent of the original. The zero value has no edges and is always at level 0; build one with NewBand. Not safe for concurrent use.

data.debounce#Debounce:
type Debounce struct Debounce is an on/off state that follows a boolean condition only once the condition has held, continuously, for a set time or number of readings.
The condition is anything the caller decides per reading: a value over a level, a check that failed, the output of a Hysteresis. A condition that flickers — true for one reading in a run of false ones — is noise, and Debounce ignores it: the state turns on only after the condition has been true on every reading of a run that satisfies the on Delay, and turns off only after it has been false on every reading of a run that satisfies the off Delay. A single reading that agrees with the current state ends the run and the count starts again. The two delays are separate because the costs are: a late alarm and a late all-clear are different mistakes.
“Continuously” means as far as the readings show. The time a run has lasted is the time between its first reading and the current one; what happened between two readings is not seen, so a run of two readings an hour apart has lasted an hour.
Readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading (duplicates, a clock stepped back, readings delivered out of order) are skipped and counted in Skipped; they neither extend nor break a run.
Method: the on-delay and off-delay timers of ANSI/ISA-18.2-2016, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries, where an alarm is annunciated only after its condition has persisted for the on-delay and returns to normal only after the return has persisted for the off-delay. The count of consecutive readings is the sampled form of the same rule, the integrating debouncer of switch-input practice.
The zero value is a Debounce with no delays, ready to use: it follows its condition at every reading. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

data.hysteresis#Hysteresis:
type Hysteresis struct Hysteresis is an on/off state with separate levels for turning on and turning off: a Schmitt trigger.
A single threshold under noise flaps: a reading that sits near it crosses it on every other sample, and every crossing is a change of state. Two levels stop that. For a High alarm the state turns on at a reading at or above set, and turns off only at a reading at or below clear, with clear < set. Readings strictly between the two change nothing. The gap set − clear is the deadband, in the data’s units: noise whose peak-to-peak amplitude is less than the deadband cannot carry a reading from one level to the other, so it can cause at most one change, never a flap. Low is the mirror image: on at or below set, off at or above clear, with set < clear.
Dwell is an optional minimum time in a state after a change, the minimum on-time and off-time of relay and thermostat practice. A reading less than dwell after the last change cannot change the state again; it is counted in Held. It is not remembered either: once the dwell has passed, the state changes at the first reading that is itself past the opposite level. The dwell guards against a fast series that is truly crossing both levels (a deadband narrower than the swings), which no deadband alone can stop. It applies only after a change: the first change, from the initial off state, is never delayed.
The state starts off. The first reading is judged like any other, so a series that starts at or past set turns the state on at once.
NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped, and so are readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading (duplicates, a clock stepped back, readings delivered out of order); both are counted in Skipped and leave no other trace.
Method: O. H. Schmitt, “A thermionic trigger”, Journal of Scientific Instruments 15(1), 1938. The deadband as an alarm setting: ANSI/ISA-18.2-2016, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries, where it is the distance a signal must move back past the setpoint before the alarm returns to normal (clear = set − deadband for a high alarm).
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewHysteresis. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

data.nofm#NofM:
type NofM struct NofM is on while at least Need of the last Size readings are past a level: the N of M of its name.
It sits between a plain threshold, which fires on one reading, and a Debounce, which needs every reading of a run: a condition that holds most of the time but not always — three readings over in five, with one dip back under between them — escalates here and would keep restarting a Debounce. For a High level a reading is past it when it is at or above it; for Low, at or below.
The last Size outcomes are kept as bits of one word, newest in the lowest bit, so an update is a shift, a mask and a population count: no buffer and no allocation, and the count is exact. Before Size readings have been accepted the window holds those there are, and Need of them suffice. NofM has no deadband of its own; the window is its smoothing.
NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped and take no slot, so “the last Size” means the last Size finite readings. Readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading are skipped too. Both are counted in Skipped.
Method: the M-of-N rule is the “binary integration” (double-threshold) detector of radar, M. I. Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems, McGraw-Hill; the same rule over a control chart’s zones gives the run rules of the Western Electric Statistical Quality Control Handbook, 1956 (“two out of three beyond two sigma”, “four out of five beyond one sigma”), as tabulated in D. C. Montgomery, Introduction to Statistical Quality Control, Wiley.
