data.slew#Slew:
type Slew struct Slew is a rate limiter: its output moves toward its input, but by no more than a set amount per second of the readings’ own time.
A setpoint or a control output that jumps — a limit cut in half in one step, a replica count that doubles — can do more harm by the jump than by the new value. Slew passes the input through, but bounds how fast the output may follow: over an interval of Δt seconds between readings it rises by at most rise·Δt and falls by at most fall·Δt, and it never passes the input. A step in the input becomes a ramp; an input that stays within reach is followed exactly. Separate rates for rising and falling allow the usual asymmetric forms, such as fast to back off and slow to return; either may be +Inf, which removes the limit in that direction.
The bound is on the readings’ timestamps, not on the number of readings: readings close together move the output a little each, readings far apart a lot. The first reading sets the output to the input, since there is no earlier output to limit. The arithmetic is the bound itself: when limited, the output is exactly old ± rate·Δt as one floating-point addition rounds it, so it never moves farther than that rounded sum. A step smaller than the spacing of floating-point numbers at the output’s magnitude rounds to no movement at all.
NaN and ±Inf readings are skipped, and so are readings whose time is not after the last accepted reading; both are counted in Skipped and leave no other trace. The next accepted reading’s Δt then covers the skipped interval, so the output may make up the movement it was allowed then.
Method: the rate limiter of control engineering, the nonlinear element that bounds the derivative of a signal, treated among the actuator limitations that cause integrator windup in K. J. Åström and T. Hägglund, Advanced PID Control, ISA, 2006; here in sampled form, with the bound taken over each irregular interval.

data.what-this-package-does-not-do#What this:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/sustain" Package sustain keeps a decision made on a noisy series from flapping around its threshold.
A check of the form “x > limit” run on every reading of a live series changes its answer every time noise carries x across the limit, and whatever the answer drives — an alert, a throttle, a scale-up — changes with it. The remedies are old and well understood: two levels instead of one, a condition that must persist before it counts, a majority over the last few readings, a bound on how fast an output may move. This package provides each as a small value type that takes one reading at a time, with the time the reading was taken.
Which to use:
Hysteresis is an on/off state with a set level and a separate clear level (a Schmitt trigger), High or Low, and an optional minimum dwell in a state after each change. The deadband between the levels absorbs noise smaller than itself. Debounce follows a boolean condition only after it has held for a time and/or a number of consecutive readings, with separate delays for on and off: the on-delay and off-delay of alarm management. NofM is on while at least Need of the last Size readings (Size ≤ 64) are past a level: it escalates on a condition that holds most of the time, which a Debounce would keep restarting. Band classifies a reading into ordered levels — below, inside, above; normal, warning, critical — with a deadband on every edge. Slew bounds how fast an output follows its input, in units per second of the readings’ own time, with separate rates up and down. They compose. Debounce takes any condition, so a Hysteresis’s state or a Band’s level compared with a constant can feed it; a Slew in front of any of them smooths what they see, and one behind a controller smooths what it does.
h, _ := sustain.NewHysteresis(sustain.High, 90, 80, time.Minute) d, _ := sustain.NewDebounce(sustain.Delay{For: 30 * time.Second}, sustain.Delay{}) for r := range readings { if d.Update(h.Update(r.Value, r.At), r.At) { log.Printf(“hot for %v”, d.InState(r.At)) } }
Time comes only from the at argument of each Update; nothing here reads the clock or sleeps, so every type is as testable as the caller’s clock is. Times are compared with time.Time.After and differenced with time.Time.Sub, which use the monotonic reading time.Now attaches, so a wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort an interval.
Two rules hold for every type, and tests hold each type to them:
A reading whose time is not after the last accepted reading — a duplicate, a clock stepped back, readings delivered out of order — is skipped. There is no right place to put a late reading in a state machine that has already acted on later ones, and a duplicate would count twice toward a number of readings. A NaN or ±Inf reading is skipped. A missed reading should not decide a state, and “no reading” is not evidence for either side of a level. A skipped reading is counted in Skipped and leaves no other trace: the state, the time of the last reading and any run or window are exactly as if it had never been offered. A series that is mostly skipped readings is visible as one.
Every Update does O(1) work in fixed memory — Band’s is O(levels crossed) — and allocates nothing; a test holds each to zero. Every type is safe to copy and none is safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or guard it. Constructor errors wrap ErrInvalid.
What this package does not doIt does not choose levels, deadbands or delays. Those depend on the series’ noise and on what a late or a false decision costs, which only the caller knows. ISA-18.2 and its technical report on alarm design tabulate starting deadbands and delays by measurement type for process plant signals; a deadband a few times the noise’s standard deviation, measured over a stretch known to be normal (Welford in github.com/org-runink/runi/drift), is the usual first try elsewhere.
It does not detect change. A deadband stops flapping around a level you chose; whether the series’ level has itself moved is a question for the detectors in github.com/org-runink/runi/drift, whose output can then drive a Debounce here.
It sees only readings. A Debounce’s “held for 30 s” is “every reading for 30 s agreed”; a gap between readings is not seen, so a run of two readings a minute apart has lasted a minute. A caller who needs to treat a long gap as breaking a run should check it (Intervals in github.com/org-runink/runi/rate watches gaps) and call Reset.
It does not reorder or interpolate. A late reading is dropped, not placed; a Slew’s output exists only at readings, and nothing between them is computed.
It never acts. Nothing here alerts, throttles or retries; each type returns a state or a number, and what follows from it is the caller’s.

data.backoff#Backoff:
type Backoff struct Backoff draws the delays to wait between retries of a failed action: growing, capped, and random, so that many callers that failed together do not retry together.
Plain exponential backoff, base·2ⁿ before the n-th retry, spreads one caller’s retries out but keeps callers that failed at the same moment in step: they retry at the same moments and collide again. Randomising each delay breaks the lockstep. Of the schemes compared in M. Brooker, “Exponential Backoff And Jitter”, AWS Architecture Blog, 2015, this provides the two the article recommends:
FullJitter: uniform on [0, min(cap, base·2ⁿ)]. The delays grow as plain backoff does, but each is anywhere from zero to that ceiling; in the article’s simulation it needed the least total work. DecorrelatedJitter: min(cap, uniform[base, 3·prev]), starting from prev = base. Each delay depends on the last instead of on the attempt number, grows by up to three times per retry, and never falls below base. Exponential backoff itself is that of R. M. Metcalfe and D. R. Boggs, “Ethernet: Distributed Packet Switching for Local Computer Networks”, Communications of the ACM 19(7), 1976, where a station that collides waits a random number of slots drawn from a range that doubles with each collision; IEEE 802.3 stops doubling after 10 collisions and gives up after 16. This package stops at cap and never gives up: how many retries to make is the caller’s decision.
Randomness comes only from the source given to NewBackoff — a *rand.Rand, or a rand.PCG or rand.ChaCha8 from math/rand/v2, seeded by the caller — so a Backoff with a seeded source draws the same delays on every run. Integers in a range are drawn without bias by the multiply-and-reject method of D. Lemire, “Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval”, ACM Transactions on Modeling and Computer Simulation 29(1), 2019. Delays are whole nanoseconds; every value of the range, both ends included, is equally likely before the cap is applied.
Backoff computes delays and does nothing else: it does not sleep, and it takes no time because no delay depends on one. The caller waits, retries, and calls Reset after a success.
The zero value is not usable (Next panics on it); build one with NewBackoff. A copy shares the source with the original, and so draws from the same stream. Not safe for concurrent use, and neither are the sources math/rand/v2 provides.

data.breaker#Breaker:
type Breaker struct Breaker stops calling something that keeps failing, and tries it again, carefully, after a while.
It has three states:
Closed: Allow admits every call. Record counts consecutive failures; a success resets the count, and threshold failures in a row open the breaker. Open: Allow refuses every call until openFor has passed since the breaker opened; then the breaker is half-open. HalfOpen: Allow admits up to probes calls, and refuses the rest. If any probe fails, the breaker opens again for another openFor; once probes of them have succeeded, it closes. Every change of state is counted in Transitions, and Since is the time of the latest. The move from Open to HalfOpen happens at the first Allow, Record or State call at or after the end of the open period, and Since is that call’s time.
Results are matched to calls only by count. In HalfOpen a Record counts as a probe’s result only while an admitted probe has not yet reported; any other result — from a call admitted while the breaker was still closed, arriving late — is ignored, as is every Record while the breaker is Open. A probe whose result is never recorded holds its place, and once every probe is held the breaker stays half-open; record a timed-out probe as a failure.
Method: the Circuit Breaker pattern of M. T. Nygard, Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed., Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018, chapter 5 (stability patterns): closed, open and half-open, a failure threshold to open, a timeout to try again, and a trial call to decide. Allowing more than one trial (probes > 1) and requiring all of them to succeed is a stricter form of the same rule.
A time before the latest one the breaker has seen is taken as the latest (and counted in Late), so a clock stepped back cannot end an open period early.
The zero value is not usable; build one with NewBreaker. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

data.bucket#Bucket:
type Bucket struct Bucket is a token bucket: it allows on average rate actions per second, and up to burst of them at once after a quiet spell.
The bucket holds at most burst tokens and gains one every 1/rate seconds; an action takes one token, or n for AllowN, and is refused when there are not enough. Over any stretch of time of length t, then, at most burst + ⌊t·rate⌋ tokens are taken: the bucket’s whole content at the start plus what it earned during the stretch. A test holds every Bucket to that bound over every pair of its own allowed actions.
Method: the generic cell rate algorithm (GCRA) in its virtual-scheduling form, ATM Forum, Traffic Management Specification Version 4.0 (af-tm-0056.000), 1996, and ITU-T Recommendation I.371, Traffic control and congestion control in B-ISDN. Rather than a count of tokens that grows with time, GCRA keeps a theoretical arrival time (TAT): the time at which the bucket would be full again if nothing more were taken. A request for n tokens at time t conforms when TAT + n·T − burst·T ≤ t, T being the interval between tokens, and then moves TAT to max(TAT, t) + n·T. That is the token bucket of A. S. Tanenbaum and D. J. Wetherall, Computer Networks, 5th ed., Pearson, 2011, §5.4 (traffic shaping), counted in time instead of tokens; the leaky bucket of J. S. Turner, “New directions in communications (or which way to the information age?)”, IEEE Communications Magazine 24(10), 1986, is the same rule seen from the other side.
Here TAT is kept as a debt: TAT minus the latest time, in whole nanoseconds, between 0 and burst·T. T is 1/rate rounded once, in NewBucket, to the nearest nanosecond (Interval reports it, Rate the rate it gives); every step after that is integer addition, subtraction and comparison, so a bucket run for years admits exactly what the arithmetic says, with no rounding to accumulate and nothing to overflow.
A time before the latest one the bucket has seen is taken as the latest (and counted in Late): a clock stepped back earns no tokens, and the bucket resumes refilling only once the clock passes where it was.

data.cooldown#Cooldown:
type Cooldown[K comparable] struct Cooldown lets each key act at most once per period: an action for a key is allowed when the key has not been allowed one in the last period, and is then the start of the key’s next period. “Restart any one service at most once every ten minutes.”
The rule is exact. An action at t for a key last allowed at s is allowed if and only if t − s ≥ period; a refused action does not move s. It is the same rule as a Bucket of burst 1 and one token per period kept for each key, and a test holds the two to the same decisions.
A key is forgotten once its period has passed, since from then on it would be allowed anyway. Keys are kept in a queue in the order they were allowed, which is also the order their periods end, because times never run backwards here; so expired keys are always at the front. Every Allow first drops the expired keys at the front, which costs O(1) amortised per key ever allowed, and the table holds only keys allowed within the last period. Sweep does the same dropping at a time of the caller’s choosing, for a table that may sit idle while holding many keys.
maxKeys, when positive, caps the keys tracked at once. When the table is full of keys still within their period, an action for a new key is refused and counted in Full: no tracked key is evicted to make room, because an evicted key could then act again before its period ended, and a cap on corrective actions should fail by acting less, not more. The cap bounds memory: Go maps do not return memory on deletion, so the table’s footprint is its largest size, at most maxKeys entries.
Allow on a key already tracked does not allocate, nor does Allow on a key whose period has ended once the table has reached its working size: the slots expired keys leave are reused. Growing the table allocates.
A time before the latest one the cooldown has seen is taken as the latest (and counted in Late), so a clock stepped back cannot end a period early.
The zero value is not usable (Allow panics on it: it has no table); build one with NewCooldown, which returns a pointer. Not safe to copy (copies share the table) and not safe for concurrent use.

data.quota#Quota:
type Quota struct Quota allows at most a fixed number of actions in each window of fixed length: “no more than 5 restarts per hour, on the hour”.
Windows are laid end to end from an origin the caller chooses: window k is [origin + k·length, origin + (k+1)·length), for every integer k, so windows before the origin exist too. A time on a boundary belongs to the window it starts. The count starts again from zero at each boundary; a window’s unused actions do not carry over.
The guarantee is per window, not per stretch of time of the window’s length: actions taken at the end of one window and at the start of the next fall in different windows, so a stretch of one window’s length that straddles a boundary can see up to twice the limit. Where that matters, use a Bucket, whose bound holds over every stretch, or both.
Method: the jumping window of E. P. Rathgeb, “Modeling and performance comparison of policing mechanisms for ATM networks”, IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications 9(3), 1991, which also sets out the boundary effect above. It suits quotas people read off a calendar or a report — a count per hour, per day, per shift — that a token bucket’s continuous refill does not match.
A time before the latest one the quota has seen is taken as the latest (and counted in Late), so a clock stepped back cannot reopen an earlier window. Window boundaries are computed from time.Time.Sub of the origin, which saturates about 292 years away from it.
The zero value is not usable (it panics); build one with NewQuota. Safe to copy, not safe for concurrent use.

data.what-this-package-does-not-do#What this:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/throttle" Package throttle caps how often something may act: per interval, per target, and after failures.
Anything that acts on its own — restarts a process, scales a pool, drains a node, retries a request — can act too often when what it watches misbehaves, and its actions can then do more harm than the fault. The remedies are old and well understood: a rate with a burst allowance, a fixed allowance per window, a minimum interval per target, a growing random delay between retries, and a switch that stops trying something that keeps failing. This package provides each as a small type that is told the time of every call.
Which to use:
Bucket is a token bucket: on average rate actions per second, at most burst at once. Over any stretch of time t it allows at most burst + ⌊rate·t⌋. Kept in integer nanoseconds as the generic cell rate algorithm’s theoretical arrival time, so it does not drift. Quota is at most N actions in each window of length W, windows laid from an origin the caller chooses: “5 per hour, on the hour”. It says how many remain and when the window ends. Cooldown lets each key act at most once per period, for any comparable key; keys are forgotten once their period ends, in O(1) amortised time, and an optional cap bounds how many are tracked. Backoff draws the delays between retries: exponential, capped, and randomised by full or decorrelated jitter from a source the caller seeds. Breaker is a circuit breaker: closed, open and half-open, opening after consecutive failures and probing before it closes again. They compose: each answers “may I act now?”, and an action that must pass several caps asks each of them.
limit, _ := throttle.NewBucket(0.1, 3) // one restart per 10 s, 3 at once each, _ := throttle.NewCooldown[string](5*time.Minute, 10000) for ev := range unhealthy { if each.Allow(ev.Service, ev.At) && limit.Allow(ev.At) { restart(ev.Service) } }
The order matters when an action is refused: a cap asked first spends its allowance even when a later one refuses. Ask the scarcest last, or use the query methods (Tokens, Remaining, Next) first.
Time comes only from the at argument of each call; nothing here reads the clock or sleeps, so every type is as testable as the caller’s clock is. Backoff takes no time at all: it returns a delay, and waiting is the caller’s. Times are compared and differenced with time.Time’s own methods, which use the monotonic reading time.Now attaches, so a wall-clock step between two such readings does not distort an interval.
One rule holds for every timed type, and tests hold each type to it: a time before the latest one the type has seen is taken as the latest, and counted in Late. Time never runs backwards, so a clock stepped back, or calls delivered out of order, cannot refill a bucket, reopen a window, end a cooldown or end an open period early; at worst they make the type wait until the clock passes where it was. A call at the latest time is not late. Query methods (Tokens, Next, Remaining, WindowEnd) apply the same rule and change nothing.
Allow and AllowN on Bucket and Quota, Breaker’s Allow and Record and Backoff’s Next do O(1) work and allocate nothing; so does Cooldown’s Allow, in O(1) amortised, on a key it already tracks or once its table has reached its working size. A test holds each to zero. Bucket, Quota and Breaker are plain values, safe to copy. A Cooldown holds a table and a Backoff a random source by reference, and a copy shares them. None is safe for concurrent use; give each goroutine its own, or guard it. Constructor errors wrap ErrInvalid.
What this package does not doIt does not choose rates, windows, periods or thresholds, and has no defaults. They follow from how much harm one action can do and how fast the thing acted on recovers, which only the caller knows. The literature cited on each type describes mechanisms, not settings.
It does not wait. Next, NextN and Backoff.Next say when or how long; sleeping, timers and contexts are the caller’s.
It does not coordinate. Every cap is local to the value that holds it; several processes each with a Bucket of rate r together allow up to r times as many. A limit shared across processes needs shared state — one owner the others ask — which this package does not provide.
It does not adapt. Rates and thresholds are fixed at construction; it does not raise a rate while actions succeed or lower it when they fail, as the additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease rule of V. Jacobson, “Congestion Avoidance and Control”, ACM SIGCOMM 1988, does for a transport’s window.
It does not judge results. What counts as a failure for a Breaker, and whether an error is worth a retry, is the caller’s decision.
It does not keep a log of actions. Quota counts per fixed window and Bucket refills continuously; a sliding window over a log of every action is exact over every stretch but costs memory per action, and is not here.
It does not persist. A process that restarts starts every cap afresh, with full buckets and closed breakers.

func Decode(text string, v any) error Decode parses text as TOON and stores the result in v, which must be a non-nil pointer. Field mapping follows encoding/json, including json tags, so a struct that already round-trips as JSON needs no new tags, and a value that does not fit its field is the same error json.Unmarshal would give.
Ordinary destinations – structs, maps with string keys, slices, pointers, scalars and any – are filled straight from the parsed document; no JSON is produced. A destination with its own UnmarshalJSON or UnmarshalText, and the struct shapes whose rules belong to encoding/json (embedded fields, the “,string” option, Go arrays), are filled through encoding/json instead.
A declared array length that disagrees with the number of values is taken as the model miscounting and the values win; use [DecodeStrict] to reject it.

data.reading-what-a-model-actually-sent#Readi:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/toon" Package toon reads and writes TOON, a token-oriented object notation that models emit instead of JSON when the point is to spend fewer tokens.
TOON is indentation-structured like YAML, with two additions that are the whole reason it exists:
name: “a scalar” tags[3]: red,green,blue parts[2]{sku,qty}: A-1,4 B-2,9 steps:
label: “first” done: true An array declares its length, and a uniform array of objects declares its field names once and then writes rows. A list of ten objects with four fields costs four field names instead of forty, which on a long reply is the difference between fitting in a context window and not.
Reading what a model actually sentDecode is deliberately tolerant of the things models get wrong about their own output, and deliberately intolerant of everything else. It accepts a reply wrapped in a ``` fence, with or without a language tag, because models add one about half the time. It accepts a declared length that disagrees with the number of values, because models miscount, and the values are the data while the count is a restatement of it — [Decode] takes the values and [DecodeStrict] refuses the disagreement.
It does NOT guess at structure. A row with the wrong number of columns, an indentation step that matches no open block, or a quoted string that never closes is an error with a line number, not a repair. A repaired document is a guess about what the model meant, and a plausible guess that parses is worse than an honest failure — the same rule [github.com/org-runink/runi/salvage] follows for JSON.

data.changes#Changes:
type Changes[K cmp.Ordered] struct Changes is what Diff found, each list in increasing key order.
To turn the tree a was taken from into the structure of b, in an order that never needs a node that is not there yet and never forms a cycle:
AddRoot every Added node. Move every Moved node to a root: Move(m.ID, m.ID). Move every Added and every Moved node to its parent in b. Each such edge is an edge of b, and every node it could pass through is now linked by edges of b too, so none of these moves can be refused. Remove the Removed nodes: by now their children are Removed nodes too, so RemoveSubtree on each one still present (or Remove, deepest first) finishes the job. Defined in tree/snapshot.go.

O(len(a)+len(b)), a single merge of the two sorted lists; the result is deterministic.
Snapshots see states, not history: a node removed and added again under a different parent between a and b shows as Moved, and one removed and added again under the same parent does not show at all.

data.tree#Tree:
type Tree[K cmp.Ordered] struct Tree is a forest of nodes keyed by K, each carrying a float64 value of its own, with the subtree sum and the subtree maximum of every node kept up to date as single nodes change.
Every query is deterministic: children are kept in key order, and every tie (two equal maxima, two equal top-k values) goes to the smaller key. That is why K is cmp.Ordered rather than comparable.
A root is its own parent. That is the usual parent-array representation of a forest (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, 3rd ed., §21.3, “the root of each tree is its own parent”), and the package uses it everywhere a parent is named: Parent of a root returns the root, Add(id, id) adds a root, Move(id, id) makes id a root, and a Snapshot or a Move records a root’s parent as the node itself. A loop that walks up by Parent stops when the parent equals the node; Path does that walk for you.
Subtree sums use compensated summation (see Set), and subtree maxima a max-heap of children per node (see Max). Structure changes cost the depth of the node times log of the branching, plus a shift of the sibling list; the doc of each method says which. Indices, not pointers, link the nodes, and removed slots are reused, so a long-lived tree that adds and removes nodes at a steady rate does not grow.
The zero value is an empty tree, ready to use; New returns the same. A Tree must not be copied after first use (a copy shares its storage), and is not safe for concurrent use.

A new node’s own value is 0, so the sums do not change; the maxima can (a 0 can beat negative values, or tie a 0 and win on key).

Each node keeps its subtree maximum, and its children in a binary max-heap ordered by their subtree maxima (J. W. J. Williams, “Algorithm 232: Heapsort”, Commun. Rescanning the children instead would be simpler, and costs O(b) whenever the maximum decreases — under a parent with a hundred thousand children, every update to the busiest one. data.treeset#Tree.Set:
func (t *Tree[K]) Set(id K, v float64) error Set sets id’s own value to v and updates the subtree sum and maximum of every ancestor. It does not allocate.
Sums are updated incrementally, not recomputed: v is added to, and the old value subtracted from, the sum of id and of each ancestor, O(depth). Done naively that loses precision for good: after a node goes from 0 to 1e16 and back, a sibling’s 1 has been rounded away from every ancestor’s sum (1e16 + 1 is 1e16 in float64) and nothing ever brings it back. So each sum is kept as a pair, a running sum and a running compensation that collects exactly the low-order part each addition rounded off, which is Neumaier’s improvement of Kahan’s compensated summation (A. Neumaier, “Rundungsfehler- analyse einiger Verfahren zur Summation endlicher Summen”, ZAMM 54, 1974; see N. J. Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed., SIAM 2002, §4.3). Sum returns sum + compensation.
The error of a compensated sum of n terms x₁…xₙ with exact total S is at most u·|S| + γ²·Σ|xᵢ|, u = 2⁻⁵³ and γ = n·u/(1−n·u) (T. Ogita, S. M. Rump and S. Oishi, “Accurate sum and dot product”, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 26(6), 2005, Proposition 4.5, for the equivalent Sum2). Every Set below a node adds two terms to that node’s sum. The first part is the rounding of the answer itself, the best any method can do. The second is the drift, and it grows with the cube of the number of updates below the node (the square from γ², once more from Σ|xᵢ|): for values about as large as the sum it is some tens of u·|S|, a relative 1e-14, after 10⁶ updates, and 1e-11 after 10⁷. That is a guarantee for the worst case, not the typical error. The test that holds the bound (10⁶ updates, values over fifteen orders of magnitude, random signs, up to 36 levels deep) also requires that no node’s error exceeds u·|S|, which holds; a naive running sum on the same updates is off by 0.1 at the root and by more than 10¹⁵·u·|S| at a node whose sum nearly cancels. Rebuild recomputes every sum from the own values and drops the drift; a tree that must guarantee eleven digits through more than 10⁷ updates per node should call it that often.
v must be finite and |v| ≤ 2⁹⁶⁰ (about 1e289), or Set fails with ErrInvalid and changes nothing. Unlike the streaming summaries elsewhere in this module, which skip a non-finite reading and carry on, a value here is state that every ancestor’s sum shares: a NaN, once added, makes every sum above it NaN, and no later Set can subtract it out again (NaN − NaN is NaN); an infinity does the same through ∞ − ∞. Skipping silently would leave the previous value attributed as if it were current. Rejecting lets the caller decide what a missing reading means: often 0, sometimes the last good value. The bound keeps every sum, and every intermediate term, finite. Unknown id fails with ErrUnknown.
The maximum is updated by walking up the same path, repairing each ancestor’s heap of children (see Max): O(depth · log b) for branching b, and it stops as soon as an ancestor’s maximum is unchanged, which for most updates is immediately.
Defined in tree/values.go.

data.treetopk#Tree.TopK:
func (t *Tree[K]) TopK(id K, k int, metric Metric, dst []Entry[K]) []Entry[K] TopK appends to dst the k nodes of id’s subtree with the largest value by metric, largest first, ties to the smaller key, and returns the extended slice. id itself is not a candidate: the question is which descendants account for most of id, and by BySum id would always come first with a value the caller already has from Sum. Fewer than k are appended when id has fewer descendants. It appends nothing when id is not in the tree, k ≤ 0, or metric is neither ByOwn nor BySum.
Candidates come from every depth, so by BySum a node and its own parent can both appear: a child that accounts for most of its parent ranks just below it. That is the honest answer to “which subtrees are heaviest”; to rank only id’s direct children, use Children and Sum.
It walks the whole subtree, O(size · log k), keeping the best k so far in a bounded min-heap held in dst’s own storage beyond its current length, then sorts that in place (heapsort). It does not allocate when dst has room for k more entries.
Defined in tree/topk.go.
data.what-this-package-does-not-do#What this:
import "github.com/org-runink/runi/tree" Package tree attributes a quantity measured per node of a hierarchy to the subtrees that cause it, and keeps that attribution current as single nodes change.
Many quantities are measured per node of a hierarchy but asked about per subtree: resource use or pressure per group in a hierarchy of process groups, bytes per directory, cost per team in an organisation. “How much does this group use, all of it included?” is a subtree sum; “which part of it is responsible?” is the largest values below it. Recomputing either from scratch is O(n) per question. A Tree keeps every node’s subtree sum and subtree maximum up to date as values and structure change, at a cost of the node’s depth per change, so the questions become O(1) (sum, maximum) or O(subtree) (top k), and every answer is deterministic: children are kept in key order and every tie goes to the smaller key.
Which to use:
Tree holds the hierarchy (Add, AddRoot, Move, Remove, RemoveSubtree) and the values (Set). Sum and Own are the subtree total and the node’s own share; Max is the single largest own value below a node and where it is; TopK is the k heaviest descendants by own value or by subtree sum; Path and Depth say where a node sits. Snapshot copies the structure, without values, and Diff compares two copies: which nodes appeared, disappeared, or moved to another parent. It is how to report what changed in a hierarchy between two polls. Bytes per directory, and the directories that hold most of them:
t := tree.Newstring t.AddRoot("/") t.Add("/var", “/”) t.Add("/var/log", “/var”) t.Set("/var/log", 7e9) fmt.Println(t.Sum("/")) // 7e+09 top := t.TopK("/", 3, tree.BySum, nil)
A Tree is a forest: it may have several roots. A root is its own parent wherever a parent is named: Parent of a root returns the root, Add(id, id) adds one, Move(id, id) makes one, and Diff reports a node that became a root as moved to itself.
Sums are kept with compensated summation, so a million updates to large values do not round away the small values beside them; Set gives the bound, and a test holds it. Set rejects NaN and ±Inf with ErrInvalid instead of skipping them as this module’s streaming summaries do: a value here is state shared by every ancestor’s sum, and a NaN added once could never be subtracted out again. Every error wraps ErrInvalid, and the specific ones (ErrUnknown, ErrExists, ErrCycle, ErrHasChildren) can each be matched with errors.Is.
Set, Sum, Own, Max, Parent and Depth do not allocate, and neither do Children, Path and TopK when the destination slice has room; a test holds each of these to zero. A Tree is not safe for concurrent use; guard it.
What this package does not doIt does not read hierarchies. Walking a filesystem, a process-group hierarchy or an organisation chart, and deciding when, is the caller’s business; a Tree is told about each node and each value.
It keeps sums and maxima only. Both can be updated along one path to the root; a median or a percentile of a subtree cannot, and needs a mergeable quantile sketch per node, such as the KLL sketch (Karnin, Lang and Liberty, 2016) or the t-digest (Dunning and Ertl, 2019), which this package does not provide. A minimum is a maximum of negated values: keep a second Tree. A mean is Sum divided by a count kept as a second Tree whose every value is 1.
It is fast for bushy hierarchies, not for long chains. Every update costs the depth of the node, which for directory trees and group hierarchies is a handful; on a path of a hundred thousand nodes it is a hundred thousand. Where depth is unbounded, link-cut trees (D. D. Sleator and R. E. Tarjan, “A data structure for dynamic trees”, J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 26(3), 1983) or Euler-tour trees answer the same path and subtree aggregates in O(log n) amortised per update, at a large constant and in far more code.
TopK walks the subtree it is asked about, O(size · log k). Asked of the root of a million nodes many times a second, that is the cost; a caller who needs it that often should ask about smaller subtrees, or maintain the ranking it needs alongside.
It is not a time series. A value is the current measurement and replaces the previous one. To attribute a rate, turn each node’s cumulative counter into one first with Counter from github.com/org-runink/runi/rate; to smooth it, Decayed or EWMA from github.com/org-runink/runi/drift; and to ask whether a subtree’s sum has changed regime, feed Sum to a detector there.
Diff compares structure, not values, and sees states, not history: a node removed and added back between two snapshots is invisible to it.

data.go-versions#Go versions:
The module declares go 1.24 and CI tests against 1.24, 1.25 and 1.26.
Go’s forward compatibility means that declaring go 1.24 is a floor, not a preference: the module builds with any newer toolchain. The floor is raised only when a package genuinely needs something newer.
data.platforms#Platforms: Pure Go, standard library only, no cgo and no build tags for any particular operating system. Anything the Go toolchain targets will build, including GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 and CGO_ENABLED=0 static builds for a scratch container.
data.versioning#Versioning:
runi follows semantic versioning. Within a major version, code that compiles against an earlier minor release compiles against a later one.
A major version is where that promise is allowed to break, and it is used deliberately rather than avoided: it is better to settle an awkward name once, in the open, than to carry it forever because renaming it would be a breaking change.
data.what-breaking-means-in-practice#What \u0:
The Go module proxy makes a published version permanent — it cannot be withdrawn, and an older version keeps resolving for anyone pinned to it. So an upgrade is always opt-in, and staying on an older major version is a supported position rather than a problem to be fixed.
If a rename is the right call, the release notes say what moved and what it is now. The changelog is the record.

data.supported-go-versions#Supported Go versi:
The module declares go 1.24 and is tested against Go 1.24, 1.25 and 1.26.
Go’s forward compatibility means a go 1.24 module builds with any newer toolchain, so declaring 1.24 is a floor rather than a preference. It is raised only when a package genuinely needs something newer, never to keep current.
data.taking-a-file-instead#Taking a file inst:
The packages are close to independent, and are written to be read. If you want one function rather than a dependency, the BSD-3-Clause licence permits copying the file.
There is exactly one cross-package import in the whole module: barn imports avro, because a barn table’s data and log files are Avro files. Everywhere else, a package referring to another — drift discussing season residuals, sustain discussing rate — does so in its documentation only, not in an import block. So taking stats or bm25 or toon on its own takes nothing with it; taking barn takes avro too.
data.what-you-are-not-taking-on#What you are:
runi’s go.mod has no require block. Not a short one — none. Every package is standard library only, so adding runi adds exactly one module to your build graph and nothing underneath it.
That has a practical consequence worth stating plainly: there is no transitive tree to audit, no native ABI to pin, and no supply chain to review beyond this one repository.

data: runi is written for code that runs inside a long-lived Go process — a service, a Kubernetes pod, an agent harness next to a local inference server. That shapes the design more than any individual API does.
data.alongside-python-not-against-it#Alongsid:
Python and PySpark are better than Go at offline data science, model exploration and distributed ETL, and nothing here is trying to replace them.
The split that works is: explore and fit offline in pandas, scikit-learn, statsmodels or PySpark; then serve, rank and orchestrate online in Go. runi is the second half.
Where a definition could differ between the two, it does not: stats.Quantile matches NumPy’s default (R type 7), so a threshold you set in a notebook means the same thing in the service that enforces it. That property is the point of the package, and the repository tests it rather than asserting it.
data.in-a-kubernetes-pod#In a Kubernetes pod:
Two things matter in a pod that do not matter on a workstation.
The dependency tree is your attack surface and your image size. A zero-dependency module adds one module to the build graph and nothing underneath it: no transitive tree to audit, no native ABI to pin, one static binary at the end.
Memory is a limit, not a suggestion. The scheduler places a pod on its requests and the kernel kills it on its use, so a library that allocates per call rather than per miss is the difference between a pod that fits its limit and one that is OOMKilled under load. That is why memo is single-flight and why the allocation counts in this repository are tested, not estimated.
data.next-to-a-local-inference-server#Next to:
An agent harness around a local model spends its time on a small number of jobs that runi covers directly: getting structured output back out of a reply (salvage, toon), retrieving context without a second model (bm25), holding one deadline across a multi-phase turn (budget), and backing off when the engine is saturated (throttle).
All four are the kind of thing an individual harness tends to re-implement badly, and all four are standard-library-only here — which matters when the harness itself is meant to stay dependency-light.
data.why-a-long-lived-process-changes-the-des:
A notebook fits a model once and the cost disappears into the session. A service fits it per request, or per tenant, thousands of times an hour, and the cost is the service.
So the packages here are built to be constructed cheaply and reused, to allocate on a miss rather than on every call, and to hold no global state that would make two tenants in one process interfere. Where a package has a hot path, the repository carries the benchmark that measures it rather than a claim that it is fast.
